sections.text: A media tycoon dies whispering 'Rosebud.' Reporter Jerry Thompson digs into Charles Foster Kane's past through conflicting accounts from those who knew him. We see Kane's rise from inherited wealth to newspaper empire, his failed political campaign, two marriages, and ultimate isolation in his massive Xanadu estate. The genius of the structure? We never meet Kane directly - only through others' memories. The story mirrors William Randolph Hearst's life while delivering a brutal takedown of the American Dream's empty pursuit of power.

Orson Welles dominates the screen at 25 years old, aging convincingly from ambitious twentysomething to bitter old man. His Kane carries both magnetic charm and creeping megalomania - watch his subtle shift from idealistic publisher to power-hungry tyrant. Dorothy Comingore nails Susan Alexander's tragic arc from innocent singer to Kane's trapped second wife. The weak link? Joseph Cotten's Jedediah Leland feels occasionally stiff compared to the raw energy of Welles and Comingore. Still outshines similar tycoon performances in There Will Be Blood and The Aviator.

Gregg Toland's deep-focus cinematography changed movies forever. Scenes pack action in foreground, middle, and background simultaneously - like Kane signing papers while his first marriage crumbles in the distance. Low angles make ceilings visible, creating claustrophobic power dynamics. The breakfast montage showing Kane's first marriage collapse through daily scenes is pure genius. Only nitpick: some early rear-projection effects look dated now. Influenced everything from Touch of Evil to Goodfellas' long takes.

Kane exploded traditional Hollywood storytelling. Its non-linear narrative influenced neo-noir like Pulp Fiction. The 'unreliable narrator' technique shaped The Usual Suspects and Rashomon. Modern directors still copy its deep focus shots and dramatic lighting. The film bombed initially (thanks to Hearst's attacks) but topped Sight & Sound's greatest films poll for 50 years. One lasting flaw? Its portrayal of women feels dated, relegating them mostly to victims of Kane's ego. Still, nearly every 'serious' American film since 1941 carries Kane's DNA.
